query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers, progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by the accumulation of dislocations at the nanoscale interfaces due to severe lattice distortion and compositional complexity. Dislocation pile-ups at these interfaces create localized stress concentrations that culminate in interface-mediated grain-boundary sliding, thereby progressively softening the material.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating consisting of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers with a nanocrystalline structure and a relatively uniform initial distribution of dislocation sources.
generation.intervention: Apply sustained creep loading at an elevated temperature (e.g., 500–700°C) under a constant applied stress, while varying the individual layer thickness in a controlled set of experiments.
generation.conditions: Sustained mechanical loading (creep test) in a temperature regime where dislocation mobility is active yet enough microstructural integrity is retained, with a controlled comparison between multilayer samples and monolithic HEA counterparts.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfaces between FCC and BCC multilayers, where dislocation pile-ups and evolving grain-boundary structures act as focal points for stress concentration.
generation.mechanism: Severe lattice distortion and compositional complexity in HEAs impede individual dislocation motion. This resistance causes dislocations to accumulate at the rigid interfaces between the FCC and BCC layers. As the dislocation density increases locally, the stress concentration eventually triggers grain-boundary sliding at these interfaces, leading to progressive plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayer samples will exhibit higher localized dislocation densities at their interfaces and an earlier onset of grain-boundary sliding compared to homogeneous monolithic HEA films. Over time under constant stress, the multilayers will show a progressive reduction in yield strength relative to their initial state, evidencing enhanced plastic flow localized at the layer interfaces.
generation.baseline: The initial state of the multilayer coatings with uniform defect distributions and defined elastic/plastic responses measured before prolonged loading.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate when the individual layer thickness remains at the nanoscale and the testing temperature allows for sufficient but controlled dislocation mobility. Deviations might occur if the layer thickness increases significantly or if the temperature is adjusted outside the defined 500–700°C window.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contributions of interfacial dislocation pile-ups versus grain-boundary sliding in the overall plastic deformation are uncertain. Additionally, the precise interplay between the FCC and BCC layers in modulating the defect kinetics requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of nanoscale multilayer HEA coatings with alternating FCC and BCC layers and a second set of monolithic HEA films with comparable overall thickness. Subject both sets to sustained creep loading at 600°C under a constant applied stress. Employ in situ high-resolution microscopy and synchrotron-based diffraction techniques to track the evolution of dislocation densities, particularly at layer interfaces, and to observe any onset of grain-boundary sliding over time.
measurements: Interface and bulk dislocation density (via TEM or in situ synchrotron diffraction)
Grain-boundary sliding activity (using digital image correlation or high-resolution microscopy)
Yield strength degradation over time (from mechanical testing records)
Microstructural changes at and near interfaces (via post-mortem microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer samples do not exhibit significantly elevated interfacial dislocation pile-up and subsequent grain-boundary sliding compared to the monolithic films, or if there is no observable progressive decrease in yield strength under the same conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling. Processing: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS software with Embedded-atom method (EAM) potential; model size 108.3 Å × 108.3 Å × 180.5 Å (180,000 atoms); relaxation via heating to 1000 K and cooling to 300 K; tensile loading at temperatures of 10 K, 300 K, 600 K and strain rates of 10^8 s^-1, 10^9 s^-1, 10^10 s^-1 along <110>, <1-12>, and <-111> orientations.. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
